overview.headline: A four-amino-acid peptide that targets the inner membrane of mitochondria, approved for one ultra-rare disease.
overview.lede: Elamipretide, known in research as SS-31, is made by Stealth BioTherapeutics, now part of Mighty Therapeutics. The FDA granted Forzinity accelerated approval on 19 September 2025 for Barth syndrome, a genetic mitochondrial disease affecting a few hundred people worldwide. It failed larger trials in heart failure, mitochondrial myopathy and macular degeneration, and is approved nowhere else. Vials sold online as "SS-31" are not the approved drug.

mechanism.intro: It sticks to cardiolipin, a fat found only in the mitochondrial inner membrane, where cells make energy.

parts.name: Cardiolipin
parts.text: Elamipretide binds cardiolipin and is thought to stabilise the folded inner membrane and the enzyme complexes that make ATP, improving energy output and reducing leakage of damaging oxygen radicals.

parts.name: Barth syndrome
parts.text: A TAZ gene mutation leaves cardiolipin malformed, causing heart and skeletal muscle weakness, low neutrophils and growth delay, almost always in boys. That is the one setting with an approval.

more.title: More: a long road to a small approval
paras: A decade of trials in heart failure, primary mitochondrial myopathy and geographic atrophy of the retina all missed their primary endpoints. The 12-patient Barth programme went through an advisory committee in October 2024 and a complete response letter in May 2025 before accelerated approval in September 2025, on a secondary measure (knee strength) from the open-label extension.
"SS-31" vials sold online trade on this history. Sources are under the Status tab.

results.headline: A tiny trial that missed its main goals, and a strength signal that carried the approval.
results.lede: TAZPOWER enrolled 12 boys and men with Barth syndrome. In the 12-week placebo-controlled crossover, elamipretide was no better than placebo on walking distance or fatigue. Knee strength then rose during the open-label years, and that intermediate measure is what the FDA accepted.

rows.name: Knee-extensor strength, change at 12 weeks
rows.meta: TAZPOWER randomised crossover · 12 people · baseline median 124 N
rows.tip: Median change: elamipretide +4 N vs placebo −5 N; not statistically significant

chart.note: The only placebo-controlled strength result. In the open-label extension the median gain from baseline was +34 N at 12 weeks (10 people), +68 N at 24 weeks (9) and +63 N at 168 weeks (8), with no placebo group.

items.t: 71 people, 28 days of 4 or 40 mg daily. No change in heart chamber volume or ejection fraction versus placebo.
218 people, Phase 3. Missed both primary endpoints: six-minute walk and fatigue score.
176 people, 48 weeks. Missed both primary endpoints; a secondary retinal-layer measure favoured the drug.
Open-label data suggested better stroke volume on MRI; not a controlled result.

more.title: More: how a failed primary endpoint became an approval
paras: Accelerated approval allows approval on an intermediate endpoint reasonably likely to predict benefit. Here that was knee-extensor strength: unchanged in the randomised phase, then up by 34, 68 and 63 N at 12, 24 and 168 weeks of open-label treatment. Without a placebo group, growth, training and expectation cannot be separated from the drug, so the FDA requires a confirmatory randomised trial, with the final report due in March 2030.

effects.headline: Injection-site reactions in everyone, a rise in eosinophils, and rare serious allergy.
effects.lede: With a daily injection under the skin, every patient had redness, itching, hardening or pain at the site, versus two-thirds on placebo (also injected). The drug-specific laboratory signal is a rise in eosinophils, a type of white blood cell.

chart.note: Twelve people received each treatment in turn, so each 8 percentage points is one person. From Table 2 of the FDA label.

disc.title: Stopping because of side effects
disc.text: All 12 completed the randomised phase. In ReCLAIM-2, injection-site reactions were the most common adverse event and led some people to stop early (Stealth, 2022). The label gives no pooled discontinuation rate.

unique.title: Eosinophilia and allergic reactions
unique.text: Eosinophil counts rose in most people treated for 30 days or more, peaking around day 90 (about 0.5–0.6 × 10⁹/L above baseline) and returning to normal after 6–12 months or on stopping, without symptoms. Separately, the label warns of serious allergic reactions needing emergency treatment, plus rashes, eczema-like dermatitis and cough appearing minutes to months after starting.

more.title: More: what the trials monitor for
paras: Allergy. After a serious hypersensitivity reaction the drug is stopped and not restarted.
Blood counts. Eosinophils are tracked; Barth syndrome itself causes low neutrophils.
Kidneys. Exposure more than doubles in severe kidney impairment, so the dose is halved.
Infants. The product contains benzyl alcohol and is not for newborns; the approval covers people of 30 kg or more.

more.title: More: the good side effects
paras: Open-label Barth data reported better stroke volume and patient-reported function, none of it placebo-controlled. The failed trials showed no consistent benefit on walking, fatigue, heart function or vision. There is no human evidence for the anti-aging, endurance or recovery claims made for "SS-31" online.

urgent.title: Symptoms trial teams treat as urgent
items: Hives, facial or throat swelling, wheeze or faintness after an injection
A spreading rash, blistering or eczema that does not settle
Spreading redness, warmth or pus at an injection site
New or worsening cough or breathlessness
In Barth syndrome: fever (neutrophils are low) or swelling and breathlessness suggesting heart failure
urgent.note: Anyone with these symptoms should get medical care right away.

levels.nopk: The FDA label describes how elamipretide behaves (peak 0.5–1 hour after injection, about 92% absorbed, essentially the whole dose recovered in urine within 48 hours, minimal build-up with daily dosing) but does not publish a half-life, so the simulator cannot be drawn from a primary source. A once-daily 40 mg injection is the only approved regimen.

explain.t: The drug is cleared within a day or two, so it is given every day; the label reports minimal accumulation.
Exposure rises 39%, 75% and 125% with mild, moderate and severe kidney impairment; the dose is halved in severe impairment.

explain.b: Why there is still no half-life here.
explain.t: The approval package may contain one, but the public label does not, and this page uses only primary-source numbers.

more.title: More: what is known about dose
paras: Exposure rose in proportion to dose from 2 to 80 mg a day in studies; the approved dose is 40 mg (20 mg with severe kidney impairment). The 4 mg and 40 mg doses tested in heart failure produced no benefit over placebo.

more.title: More: what this tab cannot tell you
paras: Nothing here applies to "SS-31" vials sold online, whose content and strength are unverified. The approved product is a preserved solution made under drug rules for a disease affecting a few hundred people.

trials.headline: How elamipretide was tested, and what Barth treatment looks like.
trials.lede: Forzinity is prescribed by specialists for a confirmed TAZ mutation. The FDA-required confirmatory trial is enrolling; the trials in other diseases have ended.

ladder.title: The approved regimen
ladder.text: The label specifies 40 mg under the skin once a day for patients weighing at least 30 kg, reduced to 20 mg daily in adults with severe kidney impairment. There is no dose escalation.
ladder.note: Patients under 30 kg are not covered. A one-month safety and pharmacokinetic study in smaller children is planned for 2026 to support a 2027 label extension (Mighty Therapeutics, July 2026).

more.title: More: how side effects were handled inside the trials
paras: Injection sites were rotated and inspected; skin reactions were treated with topical steroids or antihistamines, and persistent or severe reactions led to withdrawal. Blood counts were monitored for the eosinophil rise.

None of this is a plan for home use of an online product. The approved drug is dispensed under a specialist, with a hypersensitivity warning and a confirmatory trial still running because benefit is not yet proven.

running.title: Trials still running, and trials that ended
items: 4TAZPower: the FDA-required confirmatory Phase 4 trial in Barth syndrome, randomised and placebo-controlled, 72 weeks, ages 5 and up; first patient dosed July 2026; report due March 2030
Planned for 2026: a one-month safety and pharmacokinetic study in children under 30 kg
Ended without success: MMPOWER-3 (2019), PROGRESS-HF (2020), ReCLAIM-2 (2022)

find.text: Barth syndrome families in the U.S. can ask their specialist about 4TAZPower or the company's expanded-access programme. Outside the U.S. the drug is not approved; access is through trials or named-patient routes where they exist.

status.headline: Approved in the U.S. only, for Barth syndrome only, on a provisional basis. "SS-31" vials are not the drug.

items.label: Canada: not approved
items.text: Health Canada has not authorised elamipretide for any use as of October 2026. Selling it for human use is illegal.

items.label: U.S.: accelerated approval (Sept 2025)
items.text: Forzinity was approved on 19 September 2025 to improve muscle strength in adults and children with Barth syndrome weighing at least 30 kg. Continued approval depends on a confirmatory trial due to report by March 2030.

items.label: EU and elsewhere: not approved
items.text: The company stated in July 2026 that there are no EMA-approved therapies for Barth syndrome. No regulator outside the U.S. has approved elamipretide.

items.label: Every other use
items.text: Not approved for heart failure, mitochondrial myopathy, macular degeneration, aging or performance anywhere; the trials in those conditions failed.

cards.title: What the online product is, and is not
cards.text: Forzinity is a sterile, preserved solution supplied to a few hundred patients with a genetic diagnosis under specialist care. "SS-31" from research-peptide shops is a powder with unverified identity, purity and dose, marketed for energy, longevity or recovery.
items: The only approved regimen is for Barth syndrome; nothing supports any dose in healthy people.
Serious allergic reactions have occurred with the approved product; an unregulated vial adds contamination and dosing risks.
Three well-run trials in common conditions showed no benefit; open-label Barth data are the whole positive evidence base.

cards.title: Symptoms to take to a doctor
cards.text: Anyone who has injected an "SS-31" product should stop and see a doctor, urgently for:
items: Hives, swelling of the face or throat, wheeze, faintness
cards.note: Report a reaction to MedEffect Canada (canada.ca/medeffect) or, in the U.S., FDA MedWatch (fda.gov/medwatch).

more.title: More: what the FDA required at approval
paras: The approval letter lists four postmarketing requirements: the confirmatory randomised trial (final report March 2030), a 26-week mouse and a 2-year rat carcinogenicity study (February 2026 and January 2030), and a drug-interaction study with metformin (September 2027). If the confirmatory trial fails, the FDA can withdraw the approval.
